entries.title: Building the next generation of multimodal AI experiences with fal in Microsoft Foundry
entries.summary: Microsoft and fal partner to expand video generation in Microsoft Foundry, helping developers bring creative ideas into enterprise applications. The post Building the next generation of multimodal AI experiences with fal in Microsoft Foundry appeared first on Microsoft Azure Blog.
entries.content:
Microsoft and fal partner to expand video generation in Microsoft Foundry, helping developers bring creative ideas into enterprise applications.

Video workloads do not all start with the same input or aim for the same result. A creative team might explore several interpretations of a written brief. A retailer might turn an approved product image into a short motion concept. An application developer might combine image generation and video generation into a workflow that takes an idea from description to frame to scene. Each scenario brings different requirements for visual quality, motion, creative control, turnaround time, and cost. All of this means that a multi-model solution is necessary to realize a full vision.

Today, Microsoft and fal are helping developers find the right tools for their workloads. We are excited to announce that Kling, LTX, and MiniMax video models are rolling out to in public preview in Microsoft Foundry through our new partnership with fal. Available as a first-party Azure service, these text-to-video and image-to-video options give creators and developers more ways to utilize video generation with the experiences they want to build.

The partnership expands the choices available in Microsoft Foundry while bringing video into the broader platform developers use to build AI applications. The goal is to let developers pick the right model for each step of an experience, then connect those steps into a working application.

“fal has seen incredible adoption this year alone with generative media across all industries from advertising to marketing to gaming. Partnering with Microsoft allows both of us to truly enable the wide creative ecosystem and ensure that all AI solutions that lean on generative media, becomes a multi-model one.” - Burkay Gur, Cofounder

Bringing fal’s generative media focus to enterprise builders

fal is the full stack for generative media, built for creators and developers, with APIs for over 1500 models across image, video, audio, 3D, and generative worlds. As a truly encapsulating platform, fal provides inference, training, and infrastructure to run generative media workloads in production, while also providing innovative post trained models that pushes the boundaries on speed and quality.

That specialization matters because generative media is both a creative and an engineering workload. A compelling demo is only the start. Production applications also need to handle real traffic, scale with demand, and balance output quality, latency, and cost.

Through this partnership, developers will be able to access a selected set of video models in Microsoft Foundry, served by fal and sourced from the companies that build them. The initial portfolio gives teams a choice of models for different creative requirements instead of relying on one model for every task, with more models planned over time.

A portfolio for different video experiences

The initial portfolio spans Kling v3 Pro, LTX-2.5 Fast, LTX-2.5 Pro, MiniMax H3 Max, and MiniMax H3 Max Turbo. These models give developers different starting points for generating video from text and animating existing images. A team rapidly exploring creative concepts may prioritize speed and cost, while a team producing fewer, higher-fidelity assets may weigh output quality more heavily. Whether an application starts from text or an existing image, and what it needs in output quality and cost, also shapes the choice.

Kling: From a still image to a directed scene

Kling v3 Pro combines cinematic visuals and fluid motion with native audio generation and custom element support. Its image-to-video capabilities give developers control over how a starting image becomes a moving scene, a fit for applications that prioritize visual direction and motion.

LTX: One model for fast drafts, one for final output

For rapid iteration and previews, LTX-2.5 Fast is the speed-optimized option; for high-fidelity final output, LTX-2.5 Pro is the quality-optimized option. Both support text-to-video and image-to-video generation with synchronized audio.

MiniMax: Another approach to video generation

MiniMax H3 Max and MiniMax H3 Max Turbo are post-trained variants of MiniMax H3 focused on prompt adherence, aesthetics, and inference performance. For developers, they provide additional options to evaluate against an application’s creative brief, quality requirements, and performance needs.

“When building with video models, the details matter: how closely the output follows your prompt, how well it preserves your reference images/videos/audios and how quickly you can try another idea. Kling gives developers control over detailed reference to video generation. LTX offers fast iteration and high-quality output through its Fast and Pro variants. H3 Max brings fal's post-training and inference optimizations to improve quality and speed. Having these models available through Microsoft Foundry gives developers more flexibility to choose what works best for the application they are building." - Gökay Aydoğan, Creative Engineer

Built for enterprise video workloads

Bringing video generation into an enterprise application requires more than choosing the right model. Teams need a platform where they can evaluate different options, build with the models that fit their requirements, and operate those experiences alongside the rest of their applications.

The initial portfolio of video models is hosted in the US, and Microsoft Foundry is the first provider to offer a US-hosted Kling 3 endpoint. Key considerations for enterprise teams:

  • Data residency: For organizations with data residency requirements, hosting location is one factor to weigh. Review each model's documented data processing and storage terms to confirm it meets your requirements.
  • Model evaluation: Teams can assess quality, performance, and cost, then connect video generation with the other models and capabilities their applications need.
  • Production readiness: As they move toward production, they can use the evaluation, optimization, governance, security, observability, and infrastructure capabilities supported for their selected offering.

Pricing

Video generation pricing varies by model and output resolution, giving teams options to balance creative requirements with their application’s budget. Get started

Ready to start building? Join us at Ignite for BRK256: Video AI at Scale with fal on Microsoft Foundry. Naomi Moneypenny and Alexander Hughes from Microsoft will be joined by Burkay Gur and Lovis Odin from fal on stage to explore this partnership on Thursday, November 19 at 11:00 AM - 11:45 AM CT. Register today!

Explore Kling v3 Pro, LTX-2.5 Fast, LTX-2.5 Pro, MiniMax H3 Max, and MiniMax H3 Max Turbo in Microsoft Foundry and find the model that fits your video experience.

entries.title: Stop treating agents as one-off projects and start running them as a continuous discipline
entries.summary: AI must be selected, architected, and managed as a continuous business discipline, not a series of isolated projects. The post Stop treating agents as one-off projects and start running them as a continuous discipline appeared first on Microsoft Azure Blog.
entries.content:
Transformation begins at the line between an experiment that works and a capability the business depends on. Scaling intelligence requires production capabilities built for sustained business performance, with investments prioritized against financial thresholds, tied to measurable outcomes, instrumented for unit costs, and owned by accountable leaders. This approach manages cost, performance, governance, and reliability as adoption grows.

A new IDC InfoBrief, sponsored by Microsoft, Scaling AI Without Scaling Costs*, on how organizations are funding and governing AI, shows both the urgency of that shift and the friction holding it back.

Nearly 90% of organizations apply financial thresholds before

approving AI initiatives.

Scaling AI Without Scaling Costs

Only 17% of organizations build models to project how costs scale in production—even as about 78% prioritize cost efficiency when selecting a model. 86% expect financial results within six to 24 months—roughly one budget cycle to show something real. Together, those findings point to a new operating reality: AI must be selected, architected, and managed as a continuous business discipline, not a series of isolated projects. The market has moved from proving it works to proving it can scale economically.

Four questions to answer before your next funding decision

Run each candidate through four questions that follow a scaled workload’s life: fund it, run it, improve it, prove it.

1. How can we predict and track costs at scale?

A pilot proves the idea, rarely the economics: only 17% of organizations model how costs scale in production. Before you fund, project usage at 3 times and 10 times, and make sure spend traces to an application, team, and agent. Compare models on cost, quality, and latency, and commit steady demand to reserved capacity. If cost rises with usage while value flattens, you’ve found an architecture problem while it’s still cheap to fix.

2. How can we optimize model costs for every request?

One successful outcome can take a dozen model requests, so what matters is cost per outcome, not price per token. Ask:

  • Is routine work like classification paying frontier-model prices?
  • Are the same instructions reprocessed on every turn?
  • Is work that can wait running at a lower-cost tier?

The goal is the right model for every request, with evaluation proving quality held.

3. How can we continuously improve agent performance and costs?

Retrieved documents, tool definitions, instructions, and history are often an agent’s largest cost and a common cause of weak answers. Check:

  • Does the agent retrieve the relevant passage or the whole document?
  • Does it carry every tool description on every turn?
  • Is the same procedure copied into every agent?
  • Does it replay full transcripts instead of remembering what matters?

Trimming what the model doesn’t need lowers cost without hurting quality.

4. How can we control spending and measure ROI?

A budget alert reports the fire after it starts; a runaway agent needs a circuit breaker on every request. Cost must tie to the outcome the business pays for, such as a resolved case, so leaders can optimize, scale, or retire an agent. The business owner also needs an evaluation suite, cost and latency budgets, a rollback path, and regular reviews. With 86% of organizations expecting financial results within six to 24 months, that evidence has about one budget cycle to appear.

All four answers depend on evidence captured where AI runs: per request, agent, and outcome. If each team builds it by hand, the discipline won’t survive the tenth agent. It has to come from the platform.

How Microsoft Foundry supports continuous cost optimization

When customers ask for a few practical ways to scale AI while controlling costs, I recommend:

  • Use model routing across the over 11,000 models available in Microsoft Foundry.
  • Implement Microsoft IQ to improve relevance and reduce costs.
  • Use the plan, control, and optimize capabilities described below to strengthen operations across the organization.

Microsoft Foundry is the enterprise platform to build, ground, and govern AI apps and agents at scale. It brings together your full agent lifecycle with open development, built-in intelligence, and consistent security, compliance, and policy controls across every agent. Think of it as a repeatable production line rather than a set of one-off builds, where the same controls, evidence, and economics apply to the tenth agent as to the first.

This is what makes the operating loop practical at scale. Across the loop:

Plan: Compare models on cost, quality, and performance before committing to an architecture, and match predictable baseline demand to reserved capacity while keeping the flexibility to burst. The decisions that set your production cost curve get made with data rather than intuition.

Control: Observability that reports cost alongside quality, latency, and safety in one view, so the economics of a workload are visible while it’s running rather than reconstructed at quarter-end. That’s what makes cost per outcome a number you can put in front of your CFO.

Optimize: Model routing that sends each request to the smallest model that can serve it, an intelligence layer that provides context and retrieval centrally and addresses a common source of avoidable token spend, and evaluation tooling that catches quality regression when you make a cost decision—because a cheaper system that quietly degrades isn’t a saving.

The value compounds with volume. When every agent inherits the same grounding, governance, and cost telemetry from the platform, scaling from one use case to 20 doesn’t mean rebuilding the discipline 20 times. What Foundry does is make sure the evidence exists when the funding conversation comes around, and the levers are within reach when you need them.

Next steps for optimizing AI agent costs and ROI

Scaling AI isn’t a bigger experiment. It’s a different discipline: a shared threshold, a unit cost, a value curve that outruns the cost curve, and an owner whose name is on the result.

Go deeper with our four-part blog series on The Economics of Agent Optimization in Microsoft Foundry, which takes each of these questions from principle to implementation:

  • AI cost management: From AI pilots to measurable ROI
  • AI cost optimization: How to lower AI spend
  • AI agent optimization: How context engineering lowers AI costs
  • AI agent governance: How to measure AI value and ROI

Then join us at Microsoft Ignite, November 17–20 in San Francisco or online, to see it in action and go hands-on with the team that built it.

Microsoft Foundry

The AI app and agent factory.

*Source: doc ##US54538926-IB, July 2026

entries.title: Designing Azure silicon on Azure silicon: EDA workloads on Cobalt 200
entries.summary: Discover how Microsoft is accelerating electronic design automation (EDA) workloads with Azure Cobalt 200 VMs. Explore early performance results demonstrating faster simulation, verification, and static timing analysis, along with the benefits of scalable cloud infrastructure for silicon design and development. The post Designing Azure silicon on Azure silicon: EDA workloads on Cobalt 200 appeared
entries.content:
Every Azure chip Microsoft has built started as electronic design automation (EDA) jobs used to design, test, and validate silicon before it is manufactured. This includes simulation sweeps that run for days, verification regressions that fan out across thousands of cores overnight, and physical signoff runs that use hundreds of gigabytes of memory for a single block. Together, these workloads account for hundreds of millions of compute jobs each year. Today we’re sharing early results from our next step in that evolution: running EDA workloads on Azure Cobalt 200, Azure’s custom compute infrastructure built on the Arm Neoverse CSS V3. In our silicon design environment, the evaluated EDA workloads ran with 1.30x to 4.15x more performance than on Cobalt 100 across a range of testing scenarios, from simulation to verification to static timing analysis.

Traditionally, EDA workloads ran on fixed, on-premise x86 server capacity, sized for peak demand with periods of underutilization. The shift to cloud-based EDA on Microsoft Azure offered a new level of flexibility, scale, and reliability on compute-intensive silicon design workloads. Using Azure Cobalt-based virtual machine (VM) instances, silicon engineering teams at Microsoft are experiencing significant performance and efficiency improvements on EDA workloads that Azure customers are seeing across many workloads—optimizing the performance and speed of designing increasingly sophisticated silicon for increasingly complex cloud systems.

In this blog, we highlight results from Cadence Xcelium and Cadence Spectre, Synopsys PrimeTime and Synopsys VCS, and Siemens Calibre tools. Tools enabled on Cobalt 100 ran unmodified in our Cobalt 200 evaluation, allowing us to focus on performance testing rather than functionality.

Why Cobalt 200 suits EDA

EDA spans workloads with very different compute requirements:

  • Circuit and analog simulation — optimized for highly parallel workloads, with sensitivity to memory behavior.
  • Functional and formal verification — throughput-driven, with large numbers of independent jobs running concurrently.
  • Implementation and signoff — memory-intensive and bandwidth-sensitive, with long-running jobs.

For computer-aided design (CAD) managers, predictable per-core performance is essential to planning overnight regressions. Per-core performance measured on a lightly loaded VM does not necessarily hold as concurrency increases. Verification farms need predictable throughput when VMs are heavily loaded.

Cobalt 200 combines physical cores without the overhead of hyperthreading, dedicated 3MB L2 cache per core, and high provisioned memory bandwidth to support concurrent workloads. These core and memory architecture characteristics support strong per-core performance at high utilization.

What we measured

We tested Cobalt 200 with workloads from several stages of Microsoft’s silicon development flow, including RTL and gate-level simulation, static timing, physical verification, and analog simulation, comparing job completion time with Cobalt 100 and selected x86 Azure VMs.

All tested VMs were configured with the maximum number of cores possible for high throughput 5, multiple jobs were concurrently executed on the VM to validate the performance under high load conditions. Throughput is normalized per logical core. For the Cobalt 100, Cobalt 200, and hx176rs configurations, logical cores are also physical cores.

Consolidated EDA workload results

Workload EDA tool Measure Cobalt 200 result
Digital simulation Cadence Xcelium1 Peak throughput per logical core More than 40% higher than any other tested system
Digital simulation Synopsys VCS1 Peak throughput per logical core More than 40% higher than any other tested system
Analog and mixed-signal simulation Cadence Spectre2 Throughput per logical core 38% higher generation over generation; exceeded tested x86 Azure VMs
Physical verification Siemens Calibre3 DRC Wall time / relative performance 23% lower wall time; 1.30× relative performance versus Cobalt 100
Static timing analysis Synopsys PrimeTime4 Peak throughput per logical core 2.0× Cobalt 100; exceeded tested x86 Azure VMs

Digital simulation

Cadence Xcelium and Synopsys VCS are tools used to simulate and verify digital designs. RTL simulation is central to functional verification and can consume significant compute capacity as teams run large regression suites. When testing RTL workloads using both simulators, optimally loaded Cobalt 200 systems delivered significantly greater peak throughput than the previous generation. For the workload tested on Xcelium and VCS, Cobalt 200 delivered more than 40% higher throughput per logical core than any other system we tested.

Throughput is normalized per logical core to account for the VMs’ different core counts.

Cobalt 200 was optimized for EDA workloads through increased cache size and improved memory bandwidth per core. Our results demonstrate that Cobalt 200 design optimizations generate significantly improved performance for logic simulation workloads.

Analog and mixed signal simulation

Cadence Spectre is used for analog and mixed-signal circuit simulation. Analog and mixed-signal circuit simulation workloads differ from RTL simulation and are dominated by multithreaded performance. We tested Cadence Spectre on Cobalt 200 and observed 38% higher throughput per logical core generation over generation, and delivered 11-52% higher throughput per logical core compared with all other platforms tested.

This result shows meaningful progress between Cobalt generations.

Physical verification

Siemens Calibre DRC checks a design’s physical layout against manufacturing design rules before tapeout.

For the Calibre workload we tested DRC against an IP Macro with 16 cores per job, Cobalt 200 completed the run in approximately 23% lower wall time than Cobalt 100, equivalent to 1.30x relative performance. It also outperformed the selected x86 Azure VMs at the same per-job core count.

Static timing analysis on Synopsys PrimeTime

Synopsys PrimeTime is used for static timing analysis to verify that a design meets its timing requirements. For the PrimeTime workload tested with 16 cores per job, Cobalt 200 delivered 2x the peak throughput per logical core of Cobalt 100 and exceeded the selected x86 Azure VMs. Figure 5 compares each VM platform’s highest measured throughput value, normalized to Cobalt 100.

More than just an SoC: Platform-level advantages to Cobalt 200

A higher-performance compute SoC only helps if the rest of the platform scales its performance as well. EDA workloads depend on high-bandwidth and low-latency storage and data movement, and demand varies throughout a silicon program. Verification activity can spike before a milestone, while physical verification and signoff activity increase toward tapeout. Demand can fall sharply once those milestones are completed.

Running on Azure pairs Cobalt 200 compute with:

  • Elastic capacity: provisioning compute capacity for a regression campaign or signoff push, then release it as demand falls. Size for the workload, not the annual peak.
  • High-performance storage: supporting the data demands of large design databases, waveform dumps, and physical verification runs.
  • Global capacity: aligning deployments with engineering locations, data residency requirements, and regional availability.
  • Adjacency to Azure AI services: As agentic and AI-assisted design workflows evolve, proximity between AI inference services and Cobalt 200 compute creates opportunities for tighter integration of AI-powered reasoning with EDA execution. This reduces data movement overhead, accelerates iterative design and verification cycles, and enables AI agents to orchestrate complex engineering workflows more efficiently.

Microsoft is a key partner for Cadence, and our collaboration on Cobalt spans multiple generations of Azure silicon. With Cadence EDA workflows now qualified on Cobalt 200, we are extending that collaboration to the latest generation of Azure infrastructure and giving semiconductor teams greater flexibility in how they access and scale compute for demanding design and verification workloads.

—Paul Cunningham, Sr. VP & GM, System Verification Group, Cadence

As semiconductor designs grow increasingly complex, engineering teams face mounting pressure to accelerate silicon development while managing growing compute demands. Executing Siemens EDA solutions on Microsoft Azure Cobalt 200 provides an efficient, scalable platform for demanding verification and signoff workloads. Our collaboration with Microsoft demonstrates the value of matching the right workloads to the right compute architecture to advance silicon innovation.

—Craig Johnson, VP of Cloud Solutions, Siemens EDA

Our longstanding partnership with Microsoft is grounded in a shared commitment to help engineering teams tackle increasingly complex design challenges. We congratulate Microsoft on the impressive performance of Cobalt 200, developed using Synopsys’ comprehensive EDA flow spanning verification, implementation and signoff, together with HAPS hardware prototyping and Synopsys IP. We’re excited to see Cobalt 200 delivering meaningful performance gains generation-on-generation, including more than 40% faster runtimes with Synopsys VCS and 2x per-core throughput with Synopsys PrimeTime. We look forward to continuing our collaboration to help engineering teams advance the next generation of AI silicon.

—Sanjay Bali, Senior Vice President of EDA Product Management and Strategy at Synopsys

Designing Next-Generation Cobalt with Cobalt 200

There’s a virtuous cycle between silicon development and EDA performance: EDA tools helped bring Cobalt 200 to life, and now Cobalt 200 is accelerating those same design and verification workloads for our next-generation Cobalt products. By observing how EDA workloads perform at scale, we gain insights that help shape future generations of Cobalt and Azure compute infrastructure, with each generation helping design and improve the next.

What comes next

Our early tests show significant progress for EDA on Cobalt 200. Existing Arm-enabled tools ran without workflow changes, and the tested workloads performed competitively against the selected x86 Azure VMs. Xcelium and PrimeTime showed a particularly large improvement over Cobalt 100. Spectre and Calibre which were strong performers on Cobalt 100 also improved generation over generation, and we are working with our EDA partners on further tuning of multiple tools.

We are broadening workload coverage, validating results on a greater scale, and continuing to collaborate with our EDA partners as Cobalt 200 enters general availability.

If you’re evaluating cloud infrastructure for semiconductor design, we invite you to test your EDA workflows on Azure Cobalt 200 VMs.

  • Learn more about Cobalt at Microsoft Ignite: Cobalt 200: Delivering Azure’s Best Performance And Efficiency
  • Check out Microsoft’s silicon to system approach to infrastructure.

Run next-generation AI workloads with Azure Cobalt 200

1. Cadence Xcelium and Synopsys VCS results use an internal RTL simulation test case, concurrently run. Throughput is calculated from mean full-job wall time at the tested concurrency. Each platform’s highest measured throughput is normalized to Cobalt 100. Throughput is normalized as jobs per hour per logical core to account for different VM core counts.

2. Cadence Spectre results use an internal analog simulation test case, concurrently run with mt=16 per job. Peak throughput is normalized as jobs per hour per logical core to account for different VM core counts. The 38% figure is the measured generation-over-generation throughput improvement from Cobalt 100 to Cobalt 200 for the evaluated workload.

3. Siemens Calibre DRC results use an internal IP Macro test case, run with mt=16 on a quiet VM. Relative performance is calculated as Cobalt 100 mean total wall time divided by each platform’s mean total wall time.

4. Synopsys PrimeTime results use an internal static-timing test case, concurrently run with 16 cores per job. Throughput is calculated from mean full-job wall time at the tested concurrency. Each platform’s highest measured throughput per logical core is normalized to Cobalt 100. Throughput is normalized as jobs per hour per logical core to account for different VM core counts.

5. Results are from internal Microsoft test cases and apply only to the evaluated workloads, software versions, VM configurations, concurrency levels, and test conditions. Tested VMs included Cobalt 100 (96 cores), Cobalt 200 (128 cores), hx176rs (176 cores), and e160adsv7 (160 logical cores, hyperthreading enabled).
